name: Floss

card.summary: String for cleaning between teeth: recommended by dental associations, with systematic reviews rating the evidence low certainty.
card.note: Guidelines changed in 2015 US dietary guidance omission; ADA continues to recommend daily use.

quick.overview:
Dental floss is thread or tape used to clean between teeth. The American Dental Association recommends flossing once a day, and it is routine in dental advice. It appears in looksmaxxing lists as basic teeth upkeep.

Systematic reviews have judged the evidence that adding floss to brushing improves plaque or gingivitis to be low to very low certainty.
quick.mechanism: Floss mechanically disrupts plaque on surfaces a toothbrush misses. Types include waxed or unwaxed nylon or silk, tape, picks, threaders and powered flossers.
quick.risks: Misuse can cut gums or cause finger circulation problems if wrapped too tightly, and fibres can catch on dental work.

lead: Dental floss is a thread, usually nylon or silk, that people pull between neighbouring teeth to clean the surfaces a toothbrush bristle does not reach. It comes waxed or unwaxed, as single-strand or multi-strand thread or flat tape, with picks, threaders and powered flossers as alternatives [1]. The American Dental Association recommends daily flossing, before or after brushing [1].

For appearance, floss supports the parts of a smile that people notice: gums that stay pink and firm rather than red, swollen and prone to bleeding, teeth with less plaque build-up between them, and fresher breath. Gum inflammation (gingivitis) is caused by plaque biofilm, and mechanical plaque removal between the teeth is described in periodontal literature as part of the foundation of keeping gums healthy [2][3]. Long-term gum health also keeps teeth in place and gum lines intact, which shapes how a smile looks years later [3].

Research on floss specifically is debated. A 2011 Cochrane review found some evidence that flossing reduces gingivitis but weak evidence for plaque reduction, and a 2019 Cochrane review of home interdental cleaning devices rated the evidence for added benefit as low to very low certainty [1][4]. A 2015 meta-review of interdental plaque control and a 2020 review of mechanical oral hygiene both conclude that toothbrushing plus interdental cleaning remains the mainstay of gum-disease prevention, while noting that the ideal devices and procedures are not settled [3][5]. The 2015 US Dietary Guidelines dropped the flossing recommendation, which an August 2016 Associated Press article reported; the Department of Health and Human Services said it was not questioning efficacy [1].

chain: Removes plaque and food from between teeth
Less gum inflammation, bleeding and odour
Healthier-looking gum line and fresher breath for the smile
angle.text: People floss to keep gums pink and firm and to clear the spaces between teeth that brushing misses, which supports a cleaner-looking smile and fresher breath. Dental associations frame it as part of a daily routine alongside brushing.

paras: Floss is sold waxed or unwaxed, in round thread or flat tape form, and as pre-threaded plastic picks, floss threaders for bridges and braces, and powered or water-jet flossers [1]. Alternatives to string include interdental brushes and water flossers, which dental researchers compare with floss in trials [4][6].

Levi Spear Parmly recommended waxed silk thread in 1819. Unwaxed silk floss became commercially available in 1882 from Codman and Shurtleff, Johnson & Johnson received a patent in 1898, and nylon floss was developed by Charles C. Bass during World War II. Flossing became routine in the US and Canada in the 1970s [1].

In appearance-focused routines, floss is paired with brushing, whitening, mouthwash and professional cleaning as upkeep for the teeth and gums. Its role is to clear plaque and trapped food between teeth, where discolouration, bleeding gums and odour often start [2][5]. Some users also note that a flossing habit is easier to maintain when attached to an existing routine; habit-building writers on strength forums describe tying flossing to bedtime or gym warm-ups [7].

A 2008 systematic review found flossing added to brushing no more effective than brushing alone for plaque or gingivitis, while a 2006 review of school programs with professional flossing found a 40% reduction in decay risk [1]. The 2019 Cochrane review covers home use of interdental cleaning devices for periodontal disease and caries and rated evidence low certainty [4]. A working-group review for the European Federation of Periodontology examined mechanical self-administered interdental plaque control as one route to preventing gingivitis [2], and a 2015 meta-review focused on interdental mechanical plaque control for managing gingivitis [8].

Reviews comparing devices report that most trials favoured water flossers over string floss for plaque reduction, and suggest water flossers as an alternative for people with limited manual dexterity [6]. A randomized trial in orthodontic patients with fixed appliances compared water-jet flossing with interdental flossing [9].
Misuse can cause gum cuts, finger circulation problems if the thread is wrapped too tightly, and fibres catching on appliances [1].

A Cochrane review examined home use of interdental cleaning devices in addition to toothbrushing and judged evidence low certainty [4]. A 2023 systematic review of seven randomized trials compared water flossers and string floss for plaque reduction and found most favoured water flossers [6]. A 2024 randomized, examiner-blind trial of 270 people with gingivitis compared combinations of brushing, flossing and essential-oil mouthrinses with brushing alone [10]. No studies found examining floss for facial appearance.
